items.title: Anthropic CEO：算力是最深层的商业难题
items.summary: 上周五，Anthropic联合创始人达里奥·阿莫代伊到访纽约，与“华尔街一哥”、摩根大通掌门杰米·戴蒙进行公开对谈。 在谈话中，阿莫代伊将算力称为公司面临的“最深层商业难题”。他解释，公司选择上市的重要原因，就是增加现金储备，为高度不确定的算力需求提供更大缓冲。 戴蒙在提问中指出，Anthropic披露了涉及算力、租赁和数据中心等项目的9000亿美元未来承诺，并追问公司如何确保获得所需资源，同时控制长期成本。阿莫代伊没有逐项拆解这一数字，而是解释了算力投入的两难：技术进步很快，但这些进步将以多快速度转化为经济价值，存在巨大不确定性。 —— 彭博社、财联社

items.title: 税务师考试第一名用AI作弊，韩国启动全面调查
items.summary: 据韩国雇佣劳动部消息，在第63届税务师考试头名承认使用生成式AI作弊后，韩国政府决定立即排查2026年举行的全部国家资格考试，并计划在年内出台综合防范措施。 韩国雇佣劳动部与韩国产业人力公团15日召开紧急对策会议。涉事考生承认，在税务师考试第一、第二阶段使用电子设备和生成式AI作弊。据其自述，他通过微型摄像头拍摄试题，将内容传输给AI处理，再利用智能手机查看答案。该考生还向警方提交了自首书，首尔警察厅已就此展开调查。官方通报显示，主管部门将宣布该考生考试无效、取消其合格资格，并限制其未来5年参加相关考试，同时推进举报程序并配合警方调查。 —— 凤凰网科技、彭博社

税务师考试第一名用AI作弊，韩国启动全面调查

据韩国雇佣劳动部消息，在第63届税务师考试头名承认使用生成式AI作弊后，韩国政府决定立即排查2026年举行的全部国家资格考试，并计划在年内出台综合防范措施。

韩国雇佣劳动部与韩国产业人力公团15日召开紧急对策会议。涉事考生承认，在税务师考试第一、第二阶段使用电子设备和生成式AI作弊。据其自述，他通过微型摄像头拍摄试题，将内容传输给AI处理，再利用智能手机查看答案。该考生还向警方提交了自首书，首尔警察厅已就此展开调查。官方通报显示，主管部门将宣布该考生考试无效、取消其合格资格，并限制其未来5年参加相关考试，同时推进举报程序并配合警方调查。

—— 凤凰网科技、彭博社

items.title: The King’s Trust and OpenAI launch £1m partnership
items.summary: The King’s Trust and OpenAI launch a £1m partnership to help up to 25,000 young people across the UK build practical AI skills for work.
items.body:
November 16, 2026

Global Affairs

The new partnership will help young people build AI skills for the future workforce, prioritizing those not in education or employment.

• The King’s Trust⁠(opens in a new window) has announced a major partnership with OpenAI designed to help up to 25,000 young people build AI skills for work, prioritizing those not in education, employment or training.

• OpenAI is making a £1m donation to the youth charity to support this work.

• This is part of a wider program of nationally recognized AI qualifications that The Trust will launch in the coming months, designed to help young people stay ahead of a changing labor market.

• The announcement comes as The King’s Trust marks its 50th year and looks to the future, helping ensure young people are supported to succeed in an increasingly AI-enabled world.

The King’s Trust and OpenAI have launched a £1 million partnership to help young people across the UK build AI skills for work, prioritizing those who are not in education, employment or training (NEET). The program aims to support up to 25,000 young people over the next 18 months, helping them develop practical skills and confidence to move toward education and employment in an AI-enabled economy.

The program will help address a gap in young people’s experience of AI while responding to their appetite to learn. The Open University’s Business Barometer 2026⁠(opens in a new window) found that 68% of 16–24-year-olds surveyed who were not in education, employment or training would be willing to train or upskill to improve their job prospects.

The partnership will help prepare young people for the opportunities and challenges of a rapidly changing world of work by combining opportunities to learn AI skills with recognized qualifications and practical experience. It forms part of a wider program of nationally recognized AI qualifications being developed by The King’s Trust, designed to equip young people with the skills employers need as AI transforms the world of work.

Working with employers, AI specialists and young people, The King’s Trust is exploring the skills young people will need in a world of work where AI is becoming part of everyday life, and how these can complement the employability skills already embedded across its programs.

Building on a 50-year legacy of supporting more than 1.3 million young people, The King’s Trust wants to ensure the next generation gains the skills and confidence needed to thrive in an AI-enabled economy.

Ahead of the final report of the independent Young People and Work review, the Rt Hon Alan Milburn welcomed the partnership, reflecting on the shared ambition to improve young people’s opportunities to learn and earn.

“Young people deserve to be equipped for a changing world of work, with the skills and confidence to make the most of it. AI will bring disruption as well as opportunity, so it is vital that young people get a fair share of the opportunity and don’t bear the cost of the disruption.”

—Rt Hon Alan Milburn

For OpenAI, the partnership forms part of a broader commitment to helping young people develop the skills and confidence to benefit from AI. It builds on wider efforts to make practical AI learning more accessible, including through OpenAI Academy, which provides free learning resources for students, job-seekers and other learners.

“AI has the potential to create enormous opportunities for young people, but only if they have the chance to develop the skills and confidence to use it. We want young people to shape the future, not be shaped by it. Through this partnership with OpenAI, we’ll help thousands of young people build practical AI skills, gain recognized qualifications and prepare for a world of work that is changing rapidly. We’re incredibly grateful for OpenAI’s support as we help the next generation unlock the opportunities of the AI era.”

—Jonathan Townsend, UK Chief Executive, The King’s Trust

“Young people who are out of education or work deserve a real foothold in the AI economy. We’re committing £1 million and our AI expertise to help The King’s Trust reach up to 25,000 young people with practical skills, recognized learning and support toward education and employment. We’re excited about the talent this can unlock. Our ambition is for young people facing the greatest barriers to have a real chance to shape, and benefit from, an AI-powered future.”

—Tom Duff Gordon, VP & Head EMEA Policy, OpenAI

items.title: At Holiday Extras, dots get to work before anyone asks
items.summary: Dots deliver launch reports unprompted, flag issues people might miss, and talk through upcoming meetings on the commute to work.
items.body:
November 16, 2026

Dots deliver launch reports unprompted, flag issues people might miss, and talk through upcoming meetings on the commute to work.

Explore ChatGPT Business(opens in a new window)

Company size: Mid-market

Region: Europe & UK

Industry: Travel

Products: ChatGPT

The day after Holiday Extras⁠(opens in a new window) launched a new feature in its app, Liam Thompson, the company’s VP of AI Innovation, got a report on how it was performing. He hadn’t asked for one. His dot, which he calls Beast, noticed the launch, pulled data from Google BigQuery via the ChatGPT plugin, and brought him the results.

“I was really happy when Beast said, ‘Here you go,’ and I didn’t even have to ask him.”

—Liam Thompson, VP of AI Innovation, Holiday Extras

Holiday Extras is a UK travel technology company that helps travelers book the practicalities around a trip, from airport parking and hotels to lounges and transfers. Its promise is simple: less hassle, more holiday.

The promise of simplicity extends to employees too. ChatGPT Enterprise gives them a foundation for using AI, Codex helps them turn their expertise into working software and better customer experiences, and dots⁠ simplify all the work in between.

Liam and his colleague David Lee, Director of Innovation & Growth, shared how they use their dots as assistants and thought partners: to talk through what’s ahead, catch issues they might miss, and do work that would otherwise wait until they got back to their desks.

David named his dot Brian and he calls him on his morning commute. They talk through the meetings ahead, and David can ask Brian to run a report using connected company data. “By the time I get into the office and sit at my desk, the report is there and it’s ready to go,” he says.

When some API keys needed to be retired, Brian flagged the issue, went back through David’s email, and surfaced a list of people who might be affected. David could see who might need a heads-up without having to reconstruct it from old threads.

“The thing I like most about Brian is that he’s thinking about things that I haven’t even thought about.”

—David Lee, Director of Innovation & Growth, Holiday Extras

“My dot is my orchestrator of everything,” says Liam. Beast reminds him about replies he hasn’t sent and finds answers from past conversations. Instead of scrolling through his chat history, Liam can ask Beast when they talked about something and what the answer was.

“It relaxes me having Beast there, because I know that if I miss something, he’s probably already covered it, and he is keeping an eye on all the things that are going on,” says Liam.

Liam had tried two other assistants, OpenClaw and Hermes, but says he wasn’t comfortable giving them much information. “With anything OpenAI in our company environment, I know I can trust it,” he says. He gave Beast access to his Slack, inbox, Drive, and laptop, which made it more useful to him.

Liam talks with Beast for his morning and evening briefings. “Voice is my favorite. Bidirectional voice is the game changer for interaction with OpenAI,” he says. “It’s like having a natural conversation. I spend at least two hours a day in a voice conversation with Beast.”

Dots are also a design partner. Liam, who trained as a designer, turned to Beast to animate 3D characters for an app he was working on. He gave Beast access to After Effects and Rive on his laptop, and then watched it work.

Beast animated the characters and put them in the app. Liam says the job would have taken him several days; he estimates Beast did it in about ten minutes. “I went to university for three years to learn design,” says Liam. Watching Beast work, he thought, “Well, it’s done a better job than me.”

For Holiday Extras, the next opportunity is to help more people put their dot to work. David wants the people experimenting with dots to share what they’re learning, helping others see what’s possible and try it for themselves. The next idea could come from anyone, whether they start with preparing for a meeting, building something, or making everyday life a little easier.

That builds on the ambition behind the company’s work with OpenAI: giving people across the business the confidence and tools to work differently and helping useful discoveries spread.

For anyone getting started, Liam’s advice is to simply create a dot and start a conversation. “There’s no excuse not to get started. Really, just go.”

items.title: A step toward defining the Standard Model on a lattice
items.summary: Explore a candidate nonperturbative lattice definition of the Standard Model and how GPT-6 Astra helped turn the idea into a detailed proof.
items.body:
November 15, 2026

Science

In the first guest post on our science blog, physicist Nathaniel Craig, a visiting scientist at OpenAI, describes how he worked with GPT‑6 Astra on a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model. Craig leads the particle theory group at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and is a permanent member of its Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics.

The Standard Model of particle physics is an extraordinarily successful theory of nature, describing the known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces—the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism. The success of the theory rests on outstanding agreement between theoretical calculations and experiments across eighteen orders of magnitude, from the low energies of hydrogen’s 21-centimeter radio emission to the high energies of collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. And yet for all of its successes over the more than fifty years of its existence, a foundational problem remains: how to give the full theory a nonperturbative definition, one that does not rely on treating its interactions as small corrections. In an October preprint⁠(opens in a new window) prepared with the aid of GPT‑6 Astra, I proposed a candidate definition on a lattice—a grid representing spacetime.

I had a strategy for tackling this problem, but had not been able to prove that it worked in all the cases it needed to cover. Astra helped turn that strategy into a construction and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. To explain what we did, it helps to start with what is missing from our existing description of the Standard Model.

What does it mean to say that we lack a definition of the Standard Model? Quantum mechanics and special relativity tell us how the particles and forces of the Standard Model interact. Unfortunately, we don’t yet know how to make complete predictions based directly on these interactions. Instead, we often start by imagining that the interactions are turned off, so that electrons would no longer repel each other. We can solve that problem exactly, then put the interactions back in as a series of small corrections. When the corrections get progressively smaller, a few terms can give a remarkably precise answer—for example, it has allowed physicists to predict the strength of the electron’s magnetism to within a few parts in a trillion. This approach is known as perturbation theory.

However, much of the richness of the Standard Model lies outside the realm of perturbation theory. Take the mass of the proton: the proton is made up of three quarks, but its mass comes primarily from the motion and interactions of the quarks and the strong force-carrying gluons inside it. If you turn off the strong force, the proton falls apart entirely, so perturbation theory is not a useful guide to understanding the size of the proton’s mass. More powerful methods are needed to access information about the theory nonperturbatively, where the interactions are present from the start and not treated as small corrections.

For the full Standard Model in continuous spacetime, we don’t have a nonperturbative definition, or even an understanding of whether the interacting theory is mathematically well defined. A promising alternative is to discretize spacetime into a grid of points, known as a lattice. The spacing of the grid defines the shortest distance our theory can resolve, and studying a finite grid allows us to give a rigorous nonperturbative definition of the theory at a given spacing. It also enables us to put the theory on a computer, where we can calculate its predictions directly without resorting to perturbation theory. This approach, known as lattice field theory, has led to remarkable progress in our understanding of the strong force over the last few decades, including a quantitative understanding of the mass of the proton from first principles.

If lattice field theory has been so successful for the strong force, why haven’t we extended it to a nonperturbative lattice definition of the entire Standard Model? Here a crucial difference stands in the way: the Standard Model is an example of what is known as a chiral theory.

A chiral theory is one that looks different under reflection in space. Think of gloves in a mirror: the mirror image of a left-handed glove is a right-handed glove. If you have one of each kind, the mirror image does as well, so your collection of gloves looks the same under reflection in space. But if you only have a left-handed glove, the right-handed glove in the mirror is different.

This notion of handedness extends to many of the fundamental particles in the Standard Model, known as fermions, including quarks and electrons. Most forces in the Standard Model are not chiral: the strong force and electromagnetism, for example, treat left-handed and right-handed fermions in the same way. Such theories can be put on a lattice more readily.

But the third fundamental force of the Standard Model, the weak force, lacks this reflection symmetry. It treats left- and right-handed fermions differently, and so does not look the same under mirror reflections that exchange left and right. This treating of different-handed particles differently is what makes the Standard Model a chiral theory. And it turns out that putting chiral theories on a lattice is profoundly challenging. If we try to put a left-handed fermion on the lattice, the most natural rules give you a right-handed partner you never asked for. This is a surprising outcome, which we’ll unpack momentarily. Whatever the reason, this means a straightforward lattice formulation of the Standard Model gives the wrong particle content for the weak force. Doubling is one reason a complete nonperturbative definition of the Standard Model has been missing since the theory took shape.

To understand doubling, consider an analogy with light. Light has two polarizations, which describe the orientation of the electric field as the light moves through space. (This is familiar if you wear polarized sunglasses, which block the horizontally-polarized light that reflects off water or roads while letting through vertically-polarized light.) Although polarized sunglasses pick out a basis of horizontal and vertical polarizations, for our analogy it will be more useful to pick a basis where these two polarizations are left-circular and right-circular, meaning that the electric field is rotating either clockwise or counterclockwise around the direction of motion. As we’ve said, electromagnetism is reflection-symmetric, so its actual laws are the same for both left-circular and right-circular polarizations. (For the technically inclined, left and right refer to chirality when we talk about fermions. In our analogy with light, they refer to the photon’s helicity, which tells us whether its spin points along or against its direction of travel.)

But imagine you wanted to emulate a world with only left-circular light, akin to the way the weak interactions single out left-handed fermions. To study this in the lab, you could put a laser producing left-circular light into a box with a mirror at either end. The light could build up as it bounced back and forth, allowing you to study it carefully—kind of like putting the Standard Model on a lattice. In each case you are bounding the accessible length scales of the theory to gain control—the lattice bounds the shortest accessible distances, while the box bounds the longest distances.

If you built the box using ordinary mirrors (like putting a chiral theory on the lattice in the most straightforward way), you’d be in for a surprise: the left-circular light coming out of the laser becomes right-circular when it bounces off the mirror at the other end, so now the box contains both polarizations of light. This occurs because the mirror reverses the direction of the light without changing how the electric field is rotating (as seen from the same end of the box), which flips the polarization. This is a bit like the appearance of doublers when you put a left-handed fermion on the lattice. You supplied only left-handed light, and the box supplied the other hand.

There is a clever fix. You can make a chiral mirror using special films whose molecules line up in layers. The alignment turns a little from one layer to the next, tracing a spiral down into the film. For light whose wavelength and handedness match the spiral, the small reflections from different layers reinforce one another, flipping the rotation of the electric field in the light that bounces back. The film sends left-handed light back left-handed and lets right-handed light pass through. Such chiral mirrors have been around for more than a decade, and the phenomenon even occurs in nature: some scarab beetles have a similar spiral in their shiny shells. If you constructed your box using chiral mirrors, then the light traveling in both directions would be left-circular.

A similar trick works on the lattice: decades ago, Paul Ginsparg and Nobel laureate Ken Wilson worked out the lattice rules analogous to the requirement that chiral mirrors reverse the rotation of the electric field upon reflection. Rajamani Narayanan and Herbert Neuberger built the analog of the chiral mirrors by finding the necessary definition of fundamental particles on the lattice, known as overlap fermions. Finally, Martin Lüscher showed how to tell the difference between left-handed and right-handed overlap fermions on the lattice, while Yoshio Kikukawa and collaborators explored how this might be used to describe weak interactions in the Standard Model. However, one piece was still missing.

To identify that piece, let’s come back to our box with chiral mirrors. The circular polarization of light tells us which way the electric field turns as light propagates, but there’s another important property of the light in our experiment: the optical phase. Imagine water waves rolling past the pilings of a dock, and watch the water rise and fall at one piling. The wave’s phase is the stage of that rise and fall you catch it in when you look, perhaps just past its highest point and on its way down. For our circularly polarized light, the optical phase tracks the same kind of cycle at a fixed spot in the beam, with the electric field pointing up at the “crest” and down at the “trough.”

The relative phase of two waves determines how much they add or cancel at the same point. At one piling of a dock, two waves arriving in phase lift the water higher as their crests meet, while a crest arriving with a trough can leave the water close to its usual level. Similarly, light with the same phase in the same place builds up, while light with different phases can cancel out. In our box with chiral mirrors, left-circular light is now bouncing back and forth inside the box. After a lap, the returning light meets fresh light from the laser going in the same direction. If their electric fields are in step, they reinforce and the light builds up inside the box. If the fields are half a cycle apart, they point in opposite directions and the returning light cancels some of the fresh light. To build up a strong beam, we want the phase of each return to arrive in step with the source.

To get the phase right, we can rotate one chiral mirror relative to the other. Imagine a mark at twelve o’clock on the rim, and spin the mirror about the beam as though the beam were its axle. Moving the mark to three o’clock turns every layer of the film by a quarter turn and shifts the phase of the reflected light by half a cycle. We can set the angle to make up for the phase accumulated on the rest of the trip. Once the returning light arrives in step with the laser, we have a splendid laboratory for studying purely left-handed light.

On the lattice, overlap fermions give us a way of keeping only the left-handed fermions that we want, and getting rid of the doublers. But this doesn’t tell us how to set the phase. (The phase in question is quite different from the one we’ve encountered in our chiral mirror thought experiment, but the analogy is good.) On the lattice, this becomes tricky because the phase depends on what the forces of the Standard Model are doing at every grid point. Lüscher worked out the phase prescription for a simpler class of theories such as a chiral version of electromagnetism, but the alignment for the full Standard Model remained open for more than 25 years.

We can try to assign a phase by starting with one configuration of forces on the lattice and following the allowed left-handed fermions as we change the force fields in small steps. Now take a series of steps that bring the force fields back to where they started. The same states are allowed at the end, yet the way we carried them around the loop can leave us with a different phase. In the box, we adjusted the mirror to compensate for the phase the light picked up on a lap. On the lattice we have to work out how to compensate for the phase picked up around every loop.

My idea was to take the force fields on the grid where we want to define the theory and represent those same fields on a succession of finer grids. Comparing the allowed fermion states on two successive grids tells us one part of the phase correction for a small change in the forces. Adding up those parts gives us the phase rule on the original grid. The proof shows that it gives the right correction around every allowed loop. The correction for a change at one spot depends mainly on the fields nearby, and different mathematical descriptions of the same fields give the same answer. This supplies the measure for the Standard Model at finite lattice spacing, under a bound on field strengths at the scale of the grid.

Developing this refinement strategy into a proof required several rounds of work with Astra and discussions with outside experts. GPT‑6 Astra was essential to turning the refinement idea into a working construction. It suggested the right way to carry a given set of force fields onto finer grids, showed that the comparisons on finer grids would converge to a definite answer, and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. Human experts also played a key role; lattice field theorists Maarten Golterman, Andreas Kronfeld, and Yigal Shamir graciously spent time looking over Astra’s proof and asking probing questions that helped me to build confidence in the result. Their experience with the problem and the questions they asked were invaluable as the construction took shape.

The result is a candidate nonperturbative lattice definition for the Standard Model, potentially answering a question that had been open for more than fifty years. As with all scientific progress, however, this construction is much more a beginning than an end. Scientific dialogue among experts is required to decide if this prescription has all the properties we desire. The method that Astra and I proposed is far more an answer in principle than an answer in practice; much work lies ahead to make it useful for realistic lattice simulations. Right now I’m thinking a lot about whether this construction satisfies reflection positivity at finite lattice spacing, a condition that helps connect calculations in this lattice model to a quantum theory in which probabilities are conserved.

The construction also leaves open the question of defining the interacting theory in continuous spacetime. OpenAI’s recent proof of the existence of Yang-Mills theory (of which the strong and weak forces of the Standard Model are examples) provides the missing puzzle piece. This enabled them to prove the existence of the simplest unified Yang-Mills theory that includes the gauge fields and fermions of the Standard Model by starting with overlap fermions on the lattice and taking the continuum limit. I’m optimistic these developments will lead to new progress in our understanding of the Standard Model.

items.title: Our new blog for science
items.summary: The OpenAI science blog shares new findings, practical methods, and firsthand accounts from researchers using AI to advance scientific discovery.
items.body:
November 15, 2026

Science

We’re starting the OpenAI science blog to give scientists and academic researchers a place to share what they’re discovering with AI and how they’re doing the work. Our mission is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity, and accelerating scientific discovery is one of the most impactful ways we can work toward that goal.

We’ll publish work across a broad range of scientific disciplines, including:

• Research and discoveries: New scientific results and updates on ongoing research from OpenAI, our collaborators, and the broader scientific community.

• Methods and practical guidance: Examples of how scientists use our models for tasks such as scientific computing, data analysis, exploring literature, and planning experiments. We’ll share approaches others can adapt, including how to check the work and where a method falls short.

• Perspectives from the scientific community: Firsthand accounts from researchers using AI, what they are learning, and how these capabilities are affecting their disciplines. We’ll also discuss open questions about scientific practice and how to make these tools useful to more people.

Science expands our understanding of the world and makes advances possible, from better medicines to new sources of energy. Many of those advances begin with fundamental questions whose practical significance becomes clear only years later.

In recent months, we’ve seen an expanding range of scientific problems our models can address. In September, an internal OpenAI system produced a proof addressing the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem⁠, a longstanding question about the equations describing fluid motion. In early October, we released a broad range of mathematical results⁠. Among them was a result on the quasi-Riemann hypothesis⁠(opens in a new window), with a result that gives a tighter bound on the error in a classical formula for estimating how many primes lie below a given number. Later that month, we shared results across mathematics, computer science, and physics⁠ concerning how waves concentrate, the limits of efficient computation, and the mathematical foundations of interacting quantum field theory.

In biology, researchers are using AI to analyze complex datasets, connect findings across fields, and develop new hypotheses to test in the lab. Working with PerturbAI and Scripps Research⁠, thousands of agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind analyzed existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells in 32 minutes. By connecting the effects of gene disruptions with scientific literature, they identified possible biological mechanisms for scientists to test. Researchers are also developing their own approaches: César de la Fuente’s team uses ChatGPT and Codex⁠ to build algorithms that identify potential antibiotic molecules, which they then make and test in the lab.

These capabilities bring new possibilities and changes to scientific practice. In mathematics, systems that generate proofs raise questions about how new arguments are checked, explained, and incorporated into the field. In experimental sciences, exploring more hypotheses creates opportunities — and challenges — in deciding which experiments to pursue. Across disciplines, researchers are considering what these tools mean for training, attribution, and the skills their work requires. The implications will differ by field, and scientific communities should help shape how these tools are used.

We hope this blog helps more people understand how AI is changing science and how they can use it to explore new questions and make discoveries of their own.

items.body:
鲁比奥与 Anthropic 疑为“猎杀”黄仁勋推手

《华盛顿邮报》披露英伟达创始人黄仁勋离职背后疑为一场精心策划的“猎杀”文章称黄仁勋此前凭与特朗普的私交成功游说放宽对华芯片出口，黄仁勋甚至曾公开批评“对华鹰派”是“一种耻辱，根本不爱国”。惹怒了美国国安官员与“对华鹰派”。卢比奥借 CIA 情报撰写强硬备忘录以向总统汇报施压。

Anthropic 之所以被科技圈和舆论怀疑是向媒体“递刀子”的幕后推手，是因为《纽约时报》调查记者曾在播客中透露，他们最初收到一位“科技行业内部联系人”的神秘线报，提示他们去调查与黄仁勋有染的女子所在的新加坡公司 Megaspeed。随后硅谷舆论场（包括部分前白宫官员及开源情报分析）纷纷将矛头指向 Anthropic 的核心高管，怀疑正是他们向记者提供了最初的调查线索，不过记者和 Anthropic 均未回应这一说法。
另一点Anthropic 之所以被高度怀疑，是因为两家公司在商业路线和游说方向上存在直接冲突：Anthropic 一直向白宫积极游说，要求严格限制对华芯片出口，甚至主张给西方GPU加上“固件级锁”或追踪机制，阻止未经批准的开源模型运行。而黄仁勋不仅坚决反对在芯片里装追踪和后门功能，还成功游说特朗普放宽了对华芯片销售。

如今阻拦的芯片限制法案阻力大减，众议院中国问题特别委员会主席等人正借此契机，推动将三项严厉的新条款纳入年底的重大国防法案中，内容包括：进一步限制高端 AI 芯片出口、强制要求芯片内置防走私追踪技术，以及限制中国获取芯片制造设备。

items.body:
Anthropic前研究员再发警告：算法进步正在加速，训练更强AI可能无需靠堆算力

今年 9 月，曾在 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 从事预训练研究的 Jacob Coxon 辞职，怒斥两家公司正冲向能够自我改进的超级智能，简直是在「拿我们的生命赌博」。这番言论引来美国议员呼吁加强监管，马斯克甚至怀疑他是在配合监管宣传造势。

现在，Coxon 又贴出 Anthropic IPO 路演中的一张图，称这是促使他辞职的重要原因之一。「这张图太疯狂了，没想到他们竟然公开了。」

Anthropic 原本用这张图展示自己的技术优势：随着算法不断改进，训练出同等代码能力的模型，所需算力越来越少。

但 Coxon 注意到，图中的纵轴已经采用对数刻度，曲线却依然越来越陡。这意味着，如果数据准确，训练效率的提升速度本身也在加快。他据此认为，Anthropic 的算法进步已经呈现「超指数增长」。

Mythos 可能只是这条陡峭曲线上的普通一站。Anthropic 已经可以用远少于最初的算力，训练出与 Mythos 同等水平的模型。如果投入相同的算力，就有可能训练出更强的 AI。

而改进训练算法也不一定需要天才研究员不断提出突破性想法，这类工作已经接近能够自动化的阶段。Anthropic 联合创始人 Tom Brown 在路演中也谈到，未来 Claude 有望自行发现提高训练效率的方法。新方法可以用来训练更强的模型，而更强的模型又能继续寻找新的优化方法。

不过，这张图没有公开具体的算力倍数，只有三个数据点，图下注明位置仅供示意。

Coxon 主张应该在 2027 年暂停前沿 AI 研发，让竞争对手追上。这样会让人类水平的 AI 能力逐渐成为人人可用的普通商品，打破 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 依靠领先模型建立的优势。

items.body:
Meta、Sierra的AI「通行证」铺向数百万商家，已能对接银行转账和航班升舱

Meta 与 Sierra 联合发起的个人智能体协议 Poppy 发布 1.0 版本，开始从草案走向大规模应用。Shopify 已为平台数百万商家自动发布接入文件，无需店主额外操作。Meta 的个人 AI 智能体 Muse 也已全面启用这套协议，每次访问网站都会优先查找 Poppy。

Poppy 相当于给 AI Agent 配了一张商家「通行证」。商家只需公布一份接入说明，AI 就能知道有哪些服务可以调用、如何登录，以及需要用户授予哪些权限。接入后，AI 可以直接调用商家的 API，或者与商家的客服智能体沟通，减少反复打开网页、点击按钮的麻烦。Shopify 还把 Poppy 与购物协议 UCP 打通，前者负责身份识别和授权，后者负责商品搜索、加购物车和结账。

金融科技公司 Mercury 允许 AI 查询银行余额、整理交易记录，甚至发起转账，但资金划转仍需经过账户审批。土耳其航空则允许 AI 查询航班、调取预订信息、寻找商务舱升舱机会，并在用户确认后完成升舱付款。

此次又有 60 家企业加入协议设计，包括 Salesforce、Zoom、达美航空等，合作伙伴总数超过 100 家。

意大利数据保护局周六宣布，查明脸书母公司、美国科技巨头Meta平台在未事先告知或征得用户同意的情况下，擅自读取安卓系统用户的照片和视频，决定对公司处以8亿零500万欧元的巨额罚款。意大利数据保护局发表声明，Meta是通过脸书应用软件中的一项功能，获取了安卓用户的照片和视频。这个功能会从用户的个人相册中挑选内容，向用户推荐可发布的帖子。这笔8亿欧元的罚款，约等于Meta集团全球营收的0.47%。当局已限令 Meta 在60天内将这项功能预设为关闭状态，并须另行征求用户的同意。

—— 联合早报

FAA 全国停飞起因：换铜线升级引发路由故障

美国交通部长 Sean Duffy 11 月 14 日表示，周五 FAA 下令的全国停飞源于一处偏远设施把老旧铜线换成光纤的例行维护；新装路由器随后出问题，导致数千航班停飞。

他说根因尚不明确，可能是硬件故障、配置错误或承包商 L3Harris 失误；该路由器以每 4 到 5 秒逾千次连接请求冲击其他路由器，干扰雷达信号与飞机通信。他呼吁国会追加空管现代化资金。
